abstract: Background Obesity perturbs metabolism, resulting in differential diet–disease associations, but metabolic pathways that differ by obesity remain unclear. We investigated whether cross‐sectional associations between metabolites and diet quality differ by obesity status in 2832 participants in the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) cohort study. Methods We used untargeted metabolomics (7255 metabolite peaks) and an a priori diet quality score (APDQS) to (1) compare model accuracy and prediction, stratified by body mass index (BMI); (2) assess modification of APDQS‐metabolite associations by BMI in linear regression models; (3) identify pathways with differential metabolic activity by BMI; and (4) assess the strength and direction of associations with identified/annotated metabolites. Results In BMI‐stratified models, metabolite peaks had higher model accuracy but similar APDQS predictive ability among participants with lower versus higher BMI (BMI<25: Q 2 =0.52; 25≤BMI<30: Q 2 =0.41; BMI≥30: Q 2 =0.21). Of the 7255 metabolite peaks, 180 peaks were associated with APDQS and differed by BMI (false discovery rate<0.1). From pathway enrichment analyses, 6 pathways had differential metabolic activity by BMI (Fisher's exact test <0.05) including primary bile acid biosynthesis; steroid biosynthesis; steroid hormone biosynthesis; caffeine metabolism; valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis; linoleic acid metabolism. Strength of associations were strongest for those without overweight or obesity. Conclusions Diet‐metabolite associations were best detected among participants who did not have overweight/obesity. We identified associated diet–metabolic pathways that differ by obesity, suggesting potential metabolic‐related mechanisms perturbed for those with obesity.

METHODS
Study Population
The CARDIA study is a multicenter, prospective cohort designed to study the development of cardiovascular disease risk factors and outcomes in a cohort of young adults.
26
Recruitment was balanced based on race, sex, education (≤high school and >high school), and age (18–24 and 25–30 years), ultimately enrolling 5115 self‐reported Black and White participants aged 18 to 30 years in 1985 to 1986 from 4 study centers: Birmingham, AL; Chicago, IL; Minneapolis, MN; and Oakland, CA.
26
We analyzed cross‐sectional data from the year 20 follow‐up examination, attended by 72% of the surviving participants (n=3547).
27
,
28
Fasting blood samples from 3391 participants were obtained to complete metabolomics analyses. We excluded participants with low quality metabolomic data (n=31), those with >50% missing metabolite data (n=3), implausibly high or low energy intake reports (<800 or >8000 kcal/day for men, <600 or >6000 kcal/day for women; n=51), missing total energy intake (n=369), withdrawing consent (n=1), and who had sex change operations (n=2). In addition, we excluded participants missing the following covariate data: anthropometry (n=9), physical activity score (n=10), highest education achieved (n=9), smoking status (n=21), diabetes status (n=26), hypertension status (n=32), and use of cholesterol medication (n=9).
29
Some participants were missing from >1 of the exclusions. The final analytic data set included 2832 observations. (Figure
S1
) The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
Plasma Sample Preparation and Untargeted Metabolomics Analysis
We used fasted blood plasma samples to generate metabolomics. The full description of the blood collection and metabolite measurement methods can be found in the Supplemental Methods. The Metabolomics and Exposome Laboratory (Sumner, Director) at the University of North Carolina Nutrition Research Institute conducted untargeted metabolomics using a Vanquish ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography mass spectrometry coupled with Q Exactive HF‐X Hybrid Quadruple‐Orbitrap Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA). We used random forest imputation on missing peak data, which is appropriate in these scenarios.
30
,
31
,
32
From the 7522 metabolite peaks, 718 were identified/annotated to compounds using at least 2 orthogonal data (ontology level OL1, OL2a, OL2b, or PDA). A more detailed description of procedure for the metabolite identification and annotation have been described previously.
29
,
33
,
34
Dietary Assessment
Dietary intake data were collected at the year 20 exam with a reliable and validated interview‐administered CARDIA diet history.
35
,
36
Diet quality was captured by a comprehensive a priori diet quality score (APDQS), which is associated with obesity‐related diseases
5
,
37
,
38
and correlated with other commonly used diet quality indices, including the Alternative Healthy Eating Index and Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Index (Pearson correlation coefficient
P
<0.0001). We calculated the CARDIA APDQS (see Table
S1
) based on dietary intake by collapsing the 166 food groups into 46 and ranking each food group as either neutral, beneficial, or adverse based on hypothesized associations with cardiovascular disease.
35
Neutral food groups (n=13) were given a score of 0 and not included in the APDQS. Food groups ranked as beneficial for reducing cardiovascular disease (n=20) included fruit, vegetables, low‐fat dairy, fish, legumes, nuts/seeds, moderate alcohol intake, and coffee/tea. Food groups ranked as adverse for promoting cardiovascular disease (n=13) included red and processed meat, whole fat dairy, fried foods, desserts, salty snacks, and sugar‐sweetened beverages. Each participant received an APDQS score summarized across all food groups, with a range of 0 to 132 (higher scores indicate higher diet quality).
29
Covariates
Covariates were carefully considered based on literature
39
,
40
,
41
and have been previously reported elsewhere.
29
Covariates included the metabolomics batch number (42‐level categorical variable), field center (Birmingham, AL; Chicago, IL; Minneapolis, MN; Oakland, CA), age at examination (continuous), self‐reported race (Black/White), biological sex (male/female), maximum education level achieved (high school/college/graduate), smoking status (current/former/never), validated physical activity intensity score, with higher scores representing greater physical activity, calculated from self‐reported duration and intensity of sports or exercise categories over the past 12 months (continuous; theoretical range 0–2184),
42
hypertension status (yes/no) defined as being on hypertensive medications or having a systolic blood pressure ≥140 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mm Hg, diabetes status (yes/no) indicated by an elevated fasting glucose level ≥126 mg/dL or 2‐hour glucose tolerance test ≥200 mg/dL or hemoglobin HbA1c ≥6.5% or on diabetic medications but not pregnant,
43
self‐reported use of cholesterol‐lowering medication including statins (yes/no), and total energy intake (continuous). Height and weight (rounded to the nearest 0.5 cm and 0.5 pounds, respectively) were recorded by trained staff and measured with the participant wearing light clothing and no shoes. Body mass index (BMI) was used to define obesity status and categorized using the World Health Organization definition for White, Hispanic, and Black individuals.
44
BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (kg/m
2
) and categorized as nonoverweight/nonobese, BMI <25 kg/m
2
; overweight, 25≤ BMI <30 kg/m
2
; and obesity, BMI≥30 kg/m
2
.

Statistical Analysis
Methods of our statistical analyses have been published previously.
29
Our primary objective was to assess perturbations of associations between APDQS and circulating metabolites by obesity status. Our main hypothesis is that metabolites and metabolic pathways would be significantly associated with diet and that these associations would differ by obesity status. We used 4 analytic strategies, each with complementary strengths to comprehensively assess our objective: (1) orthogonal partial least squares–regression (OPLS‐R) analysis to evaluate the ability of metabolomic data to explain APDQS for each level of obesity; (2) multivariable‐adjusted linear regression models with metabolite peaks (n=7522 peaks) to investigate whether associations between APDQS and metabolite peaks differed by obesity status; (3) metabolomic pathway enrichment analysis to identify metabolic pathways perturbed by obesity; and (4) multivariable‐adjusted linear regression models with identified/annotated metabolites (n=18 metabolites) to assess directionality and strength of associations between APDQS and specific metabolites. We used SIMCA software version 17 (Sartorius AG) for the OPLS‐R analyses, SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) for multivariable‐adjusted linear regression models, and the Mummichog algorithm (version 2.0) within the MetaboAnalyst software version 5.0 (
https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/
) for pathway enrichment analyses.
Orthogonal partial least squares–regression: We used OPLS‐R to assess the ability of untargeted metabolomics to explain variation in APDQS.
45
Briefly, OPLS‐R seeks to maximize the variance explained in a continuous variable (i.e., APDQS) by using multivariate data (i.e., metabolite peaks).
46
OPLS‐R uses cross‐validation methods to minimize overfitting. As an additional precaution, we separated our dataset into test and training datasets to assess model predictability and accuracy. We used the training dataset (a randomly selected subset of 70% of our sample) for OPLS‐R modeling and the test dataset (remaining 30% of our sample) to evaluate model fit. To quantify how well metabolomics explain variation in APDQS, OPLS‐R uses root mean squared error (rMSE) to assess model accuracy
47
and calculates the Q
2
value using cross‐validation methods (referred to as the “cross‐validated R
2
”) to assess the predictive ability. Higher Q
2
values indicate better predictive ability with a Q
2
value of 1 indicating 100% accuracy from cross‐validation. Q
2
values >0.4 are considered adequate.
48
,
49
,
50
In addition to cross‐validation, permutation‐based validation with 1000 iterations was used to assess whether the OPLS‐R models were overfitted. Because OPLS methods do not allow explicit testing for interactions, we ran OPLS‐R models stratified by obesity status and calculated T1 vector scores separately by each obesity status: nonoverweight/nonobese, BMI <25 kg/m
2
; overweight, 25≤ BMI <30 kg/m
2
; and obesity, BMI≥30 kg/m
2
. T1 scores represent the linear combination of all 7522 metabolite peaks that explain the most variation in APDQS. To evaluate the accuracy of the OPLS‐R models, we used normalized rMSE, calculated by dividing the rMSE by the difference of the range (maximum–minimum),
51
for the test and training data sets separately to directly compare model accuracy across BMI groups.
Linear regression models (n=7255 metabolite peaks): We next used generalized linear regression models (PROC GLM, SAS 9.4, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) to estimate associations between APDQS (continuous) and each of the 7522 metabolite peaks, separately, and to investigate whether associations differed by obesity status. Our fully adjusted model included the metabolomics batch number, study field center, total energy intake, age, sex, self‐reported race, maximum education level, smoking status, physical activity score, diabetes status, hypertension status, and self‐reported use of cholesterol lowering medication.
29
We conducted additional sensitivity analyses (Models 1–3) to assess whether our results were robust after adjusting for different covariates and to parse out the influence of nonmodifiable, lifestyle, or clinical variables, separately, on the association between metabolites and diet quality. Model 1 included study sample metabolomics data acquisition batch number, study field center, total energy intake, age, sex, self‐reported race, and maximum education level. Model 2 included covariates in Model 1, with further adjustment for lifestyle factors including smoking status, and physical activity score. Model 3 included covariates in Model 1, with further adjustment for health status variables including diabetes status, hypertension status, and self‐reported use of cholesterol lowering medication. Model 4 (fully adjusted model) included all covariates in Models 1 to 3. To determine whether BMI modifies the association between APDQS and metabolite peaks, we included an interaction term between BMI and each metabolite peak for all models.
Metabolomic pathway enrichment analyses: We conducted metabolomic pathway enrichment analyses to contextualize our findings from linear regression models and to identify metabolic pathways perturbed by obesity. We used metabolite features to conduct pathway analyses using the Mummichog algorithm (version 2) within the MS Peaks to Pathways Functional Analyses module within the MetaboAnalyst software (version 5).
29
,
52
In this study, metabolomic pathway analysis identifies significantly enriched metabolomic pathways based on results from OPLS‐R or multivariable‐adjusted linear regression models. Pathways are considered enriched if there are more metabolically active compounds within the pathway than expected by chance using a Fisher's exact test (FET) ≤0.05.
52
Pathway analysis calculates an enrichment factor, defined as the ratio of the number of metabolite peaks observed as enriched versus expected in a pathway, with larger factors indicating greater pathway activity. Specifically, pathway enrichment was defined based on variable influence on projection scores from OPLS‐R models or
P
values from the metabolite‐BMI interaction term from the linear regression models.
52
We included these scores or
P
values along with metabolite peak mass‐to‐charge ratio (m/z) in the MetaboAnalyst software to conduct pathway analysis. Specifically,
P
values <0.05 for the interaction term in linear regression models and variable influence on projection scores >1.5 and FET <0.05 from OPLS‐R models were used as thresholds of significance to identify perturbed metabolomic pathways. Analyses were conducted in positive ion mode with a 3 ppm mass tolerance and based on pathways in the human Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes database (release 102.0).
53
,
54
Although linear regression models with metabolite peaks paired with pathway enrichment analyses can highlight which pathways have differential metabolic activity, these results cannot determine the direction or strength of associations.
Fully adjusted linear regression models with identified/annotated metabolites: We then conducted linear regression models with identified/annotated metabolites which allowed us to assess directionality and strength of associations between specific metabolites and APDQS. From the 7522 metabolite peaks, 718 were identified/annotated by automated data analysis pipeline to compounds using at least 2 orthogonal data (ontology level OL1, OL2a, OL2b, or PDA). We merged the list of identified/annotated metabolites (n=718) with those metabolite peaks that were significantly associated (false discovery rate <0.1) with APDQS in the fully adjusted model (n=180 peaks). A false discovery rate threshold between 5% and 10% is commonly used in ‐omics literature.
55
Therefore, we used a false discovery rate <0.1 as a conservative approach to ensure adequate statistical power to detect effect modification. The merged list resulted in 18 identified/annotated metabolites that we then ran through fully adjusted linear regression models with an interaction term between each metabolite and the mean value of each obesity status. To illustrate the potential differences in strength and direction of associations between these identified/annotated metabolites and APDQS, we calculated adjusted estimates of APDQS from fully adjusted linear regression models (PROC GLM, SAS 9.4, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) with a metabolite‐BMI interaction term. Given that BMI was used as a continuous variable in the linear regression models, we estimated the change in APDQS for a 1‐unit increase for each metabolite using the mean BMI value for each obesity status. The mean BMI for each category was nonoverweight/nonobese (22.4 kg/m
2
), overweight (27.5 kg/m
2
), and obesity (36.3 kg/m
2
).
Ethical Considerations and Approvals
Study participants provided informed consent at each examination and the institutional review board at each CARDIA site approved the exam protocols. The CARDIA Steering Committee and the institutional review board at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill approved this secondary analysis. We used the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiologycohort checklist when writing our report.

Research Perspective
What Is New?
Metabolic pathways associated with diet differed by body mass index status.
What Question Should Be Addressed Next?
Our findings identify possible perturbations in metabolism by obesity.
Future mechanistic‐based research should focus on specific metabolites disrupted by obesity.
Higher diet quality, as defined by higher consumption of whole fruits and vegetables, nuts and legumes, lean meats, and fatty fish, is beneficial for preventing metabolic diseases, especially among early‐to‐middle aged adults.
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
However, there is interindividual variability in how diet is metabolized, which leads to heterogeneity in associations between diet and metabolic diseases.
6
Identifying factors that affect interindividual variability in the response to diet can improve precision of dietary recommendations, inform clinical care guidelines, and highlight targets for drug interventions.
Obesity is a complex disease strongly correlated with diet and metabolic diseases including type 2 diabetes,
7
,
8
certain cancers,
9
,
10
and cardiovascular disease.
11
,
12
However, in some studies, associations between diet, obesity status, and obesity‐related diseases are often heterogeneous, which may be due to underlying differences in metabolism.
13
Obesity, as defined by having excess adiposity, is thought to perturb underlying pathways of metabolism.
14
,
15
For example, obesity has been associated with metabolic alterations in insulin resistance,
7
,
8
inflammation,
16
and altered gene expression,
17
which may in turn impact dietary effects on metabolic outcomes. However, these relationships are complex, and more research is critically needed to improve our understanding. Assessing perturbations in diet‐associated metabolic pathways by obesity status can provide insight into modifiable mechanisms to target and prevent metabolic disease.
Metabolomics is a useful tool that identifies small molecules (i.e., metabolites) in biological samples and can uncover underlying biochemical pathways important in disease mechanisms. Metabolomics captures the downstream effects of genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics and is associated with exogenous inputs such as diet.
18
Others have successfully used metabolomics to characterize diet
19
,
20
and to identify potential metabolic signatures of obesity.
13
,
14
,
15
However, previous studies have not fully elucidated underlying metabolic pathways because they used targeted metabolomics (rather than untargeted) and focused on single nutrients or metabolites, which limits the power to detect diet‐related associations and may miss important metabolic patterns and pathways.
20
,
21
,
22
,
23
We need research using untargeted metabolomics, capturing the widest range of metabolites potentially associated with diet, to generate hypotheses and examine mechanisms of the heterogeneity in diet–metabolite associations by obesity status.
24
In this study, we investigated cross‐sectional associations between untargeted metabolomics data and diet quality with potential differences by obesity status in the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study at year 20 of follow‐up (2005–2006). This study was motivated by the need to examine metabolic reasons for observed heterogeneity by obesity in large, diverse populations. CARDIA is a multicenter, population‐based cohort of Black and White Americans aged 37 to 55 years with extensive diet data and untargeted metabolomics from blood samples.
25
Current dietary recommendations for chronic disease prevention are broad and applied to the entire population, thus ignoring specificity by obesity status. Combining untargeted metabolomic and comprehensive dietary intake data to understand metabolic differences by obesity status can improve the effectiveness of nutrition recommendations and dietary interventions for individuals with obesity. We hypothesized that metabolites and metabolic pathways would be significantly associated with diet and that these associations would differ by obesity status. Our findings could inform diet‐disease pathogenesis and prognosis and could potentially point to targetable pathways for drug development, screening tools, and precision nutritional recommendations by obesity status.

Given that BMI was used as a continuous variable in the linear regression models, we estimated the change in APDQS for a 1‐unit increase for each metabolite using the mean BMI value for each obesity status. The mean BMI for each category was nonoverweight/nonobese (22.4 kg/m
2
), overweight (27.5 kg/m
2
), and obesity (36.3 kg/m
2
).

Linear Regression Models (n=7255 Metabolite Peaks): Assessing the Degree to Ehich Obesity Perturbs the
APDQS
‐Associated Metabolome
We ran multivariable‐adjusted linear regression models with all 7255 metabolite peaks to determine if associations between metabolite peaks and APDQS differed significantly by obesity status. From our fully adjusted model, we found 180 metabolites peaks that were associated with APDQS and that differed significantly by obesity (false discovery rate <0.1). Although these results indicate the degree of perturbation of diet–metabolite associations by obesity, they do not identify which pathways are perturbed. Therefore, we conducted subsequent metabolic pathway enrichment analyses to contextualize our results from the fully adjusted model and to identify metabolic pathways perturbed by obesity.
Metabolomic Pathway Enrichment Analyses: Identifying
APDQS
‐Associated Metabolomic Pathways Perturbed by Obesity
For metabolomic pathway enrichment analysis, we mapped all 7522 metabolite peaks onto their respective metabolic pathways to identify pathways associated with APDQS that had differential metabolic activity by obesity status. We calculated an enrichment factor to assess the amount of metabolic activity within each pathway, with higher factors indicating greater pathway activity, and used an FET<0.05 to determine whether pathway activity was higher than expected by chance. We found a total of 63 enriched metabolic pathways from the fully adjusted model (model 4). A comparison of the enriched pathways from the fully adjusted and sensitivity models are listed in Table
S3
and Figure
S3
. Enrichment was defined as having more compounds detected within a pathway than expected by chance, using the threshold of FET<0.05 (Table
S3
). From the fully adjusted model, 6 pathways had differential metabolic activity (FET<0.05) by obesity status, including primary bile acid biosynthesis; steroid biosynthesis; steroid hormone biosynthesis; caffeine metabolism; valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis; and linoleic acid metabolism (Figure
2
). Pathway results were similar across other sensitivity models; however, without accounting for lifestyle variables, such as smoking status or physical activity level, and health status, such as hypertension, diabetes, or self‐reported use of cholesterol‐lowering medications, the only pathway that remained significantly associated with APDQS was D‐glutamine and D‐glutamate metabolism (Figure
S4
). After accounting for health status but not lifestyle variables, biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids became significant (Figure
S5
). After accounting for lifestyle but not health status variables, tyrosine metabolism became significant (Figure
S6
).

We also conducted pathway enrichment analysis using our OPLS‐R results. From OPLS‐R pathway analysis, we identified the pathways associated with APDQS separately by each obesity status using training data from 70% of all samples based on variable influence on projection scores >1.5 and FET <0.05. We found that OPLS‐R pathway analyses supported our findings from linear regression models. Of the 6 pathways found previously that significantly differed by obesity status, linoleic acid metabolism, primary bile acid biosynthesis, steroid biosynthesis and steroid hormone biosynthesis uniquely differed for participants with obesity. Through OPLS‐R pathway enrichment, we found additional pathways that uniquely differed for those with overweight or obesity included caffeine metabolism, biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids, retinol metabolism, and terpenoid backbone biosynthesis.

DISCUSSION
We investigated whether obesity status modified the association between diet quality, indicated with the APDQS, and untargeted metabolomics in 2832 participants in the CARDIA study. Overall, we found that (1) untargeted metabolomics better explain variability and discriminate APDQS for participants with nonoverweight/nonobesity status compared with participants with overweight/obesity status; (2) BMI modified the association between APDQS and metabolite peaks after adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and health status covariates; and (3) metabolic pathways and annotated metabolites for which BMI modified the association between diet quality and metabolite peaks are involved in omega‐6 PUFA metabolism (eg, linoleic acid), branched‐chain amino acids (eg, leucine, isoleucine, and valine biosynthesis), and cholesterol metabolism (eg, primary bile acid biosynthesis, steroid biosynthesis, and steroid hormone biosynthesis).
Previous studies have found that obesity status significantly perturbs the metabolome and that the metabolic response to diet differs across individuals with and without obesity.
13
,
14
,
15
,
57
,
58
,
59
Among healthy individuals, dietary intake and the blood metabolome are highly correlated, with diet contributing up to 50% of the total variation in blood metabolites.
60
However, the strength of the correlation between the metabolome and diet differs widely between individuals and may depend on obesity status.
14
Our results support the hypothesis that obesity disrupts the correlation between diet and the metabolome. From OPLS‐R using all 7522 metabolite peaks, we found lower model predictive ability of diet–metabolite associations for those with obesity and overweight compared with those without obesity. Reasons for these perturbations might be related to obesity's effect on systemic inflammation,
16
insulin resistance,
7
,
8
and altered gene expression,
17
which together could alter the dietary impact on the metabolome. In addition to the perturbed associations between metabolites and diet among those with obesity, there is also evidence that specific metabolic pathways are disrupted by obesity. Our pathway enrichment analyses revealed several key metabolic pathways that were perturbed by obesity status, namely pathways involved in omega‐6 PUFA metabolism (eg, linoleic acid), branched‐chain amino acids (eg, leucine, isoleucine, and valine biosynthesis), and cholesterol metabolism (eg, primary bile acid biosynthesis, steroid biosynthesis, and steroid hormone biosynthesis).
Several studies have investigated alterations in dietary response and fatty acid metabolism by obesity status and adipose tissue type.
58
,
59
,
61
,
62
,
63
Fatty acids, particularly those involved in PUFA metabolism, are widely recognized for their effects on systemic inflammation, glycemic control, and adipose tissue function.
62
,
64
,
65
,
66
In a dietary intervention study comparing 3 obesity groups, consumption of a standardized diet resulted in significant differences in concentrations of several fatty acids, including linoleic acid, γ‐linolenic acid, arachidonic acid, and palmitoleic acid.
58
Similarly, we found that the association between linoleic acid (omega‐6 PUFA) metabolism (FET
P
=0.04) and APDQS differed significantly by obesity status. In nonadjusted OPLS‐R stratified models, linoleic metabolism was most enriched for those with overweight status (enrichment factor=5.14, FET
P
=0.01) but not enriched among participants without overweight/obesity or with obesity. For linolenic acid (omega‐3 PUFA) metabolism, we did not observe statistically significant differences by obesity in our pathway enrichment models (FET=0.74; Table
S3
). However, results from annotated metabolites suggested that every 2‐fold change in linolenic acid, the APDQS lowered by 3.56, 2.57, but only 0.83 points for those with a mean BMI of 22.4 kg/m
2
, 27.5 kg/m
2
, and 36.3 kg/m
2
, respectively. Mechanisms of how obesity disrupts diet–metabolism associations are complex. However, our study and others suggest that increased levels of systemic inflammation, amplified among those with obesity, can lead to dysregulation of inflammation‐associated metabolic pathways, including PUFA metabolism.
16
,
17
Obesity status, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes have been associated with elevated fasted levels of branched chain amino acids, including valine, leucine, and isoleucine.
67
,
68
In a study of twins discordant for obesity, fasted levels of branched‐chain amino acids (valine and isoleucine) were higher for discordant heavier twins (BMI mean±SD: 30.6±5.1 kg/m
2
) compared with discordant leaner twins (BMI mean±SD: 24.8±3.9 kg/m
2
).
59
In our study, branched‐chain amino acid biosynthesis associated with diet quality had differential pathway enrichment by obesity status in pathway analyses based on results from fully adjusted linear regression models (enrichment factor=2.76, FET
P
=0.03). However, branched‐chain amino acid biosynthesis was not significantly enriched at any obesity status in nonadjusted OPLS‐R models that did not control for covariates. In a study comparing adipose‐derived metabolites in participants with and without obesity using untargeted gas chromatography‐mass spectrometry‐based metabolomics, most metabolites that differed by obesity status included the branched‐chain amino acid leucine, as well as other essential amino acids (lysine, methionine, and threonine) and nonessential amino acids (alanine, glutamine, and serine).
69
In particular, leucine metabolism was dysregulated with decreased leucine uptake and degradation found in visceral obese but not nonobese adipose tissue.
69
Furthermore, their results found that differences in metabolites were determined by overall obesity status rather than location of adipose tissue (visceral versus subcutaneous).
69
The most consistent differences in associations between the fasted plasma metabolome and diet quality by obesity status in our study were observed for cholesterol metabolism pathways, including primary bile acid biosynthesis, steroid biosynthesis, and steroid hormone biosynthesis. Bile acids can sense circulating nutrients and function as metabolic regulators of lipids and energy status.
69
,
70
Metabolic syndrome, including obesity and insulin resistance, is associated with dysregulation of bile acid production and signaling.
70
In our study, primary bile acid biosynthesis associated with diet quality had differential pathway enrichment by obesity status in linear regression pathway analyses. In nonadjusted stratified models, OPLS‐R pathway analyses revealed that primary bile acid biosynthesis was a significant predictor of diet quality among participants without overweight/obesity but not for participants with overweight or obesity. Correlations between the bile acids and diet are greatly influenced by the gut microbiome,
70
,
71
which we unfortunately could not account for in this study. However, in the study of postprandial responses of discordant twins, Bondia‐Pons et al. found no differences in stool bacterial diversity between twins discordant by weight, suggesting that metabolomic differences were not related to genetic and microbial factors.
72
Limitations
We were unable to identify/annotate all metabolite peaks in our data set, as is typical in untargeted metabolomics analyses.
73
The current platform cannot differentiate isomer(s) of the reference standard peaks, and therefore multiple peaks may be annotated with the same compound name. Although we investigated associations using all 7522 metabolite peaks, it is possible that multiple peaks are associated with different adducts for the same compound, which could introduce redundancy in our regression models. To address the issue of many‐to‐many matching, we used the mummichog algorithm within the MetaboAnalyst software, which was developed specifically to address this issue of duplicate annotations within metabolic pathways. Additionally, because we could not match all significant metabolite peaks to an annotated metabolite, we cannot interpret the annotated metabolites as a comprehensive list of all metabolites that could possibly differ by BMI. However, we will have more data available to investigate these questions as more metabolite peaks are annotated and identified.
In addition, we acknowledge that while BMI is easily measured, cost effective, and has been consistently associated with mortality and chronic diseases, it does not distinguish between body mass type (eg, fat, bone density, muscle), fat mass distribution, or differences in fat tissue (eg, visceral versus subcutaneous).
74
However, despite BMI capturing body mass as opposed to adiposity, it is the most commonly used tool to measure obesity status and has been independently associated with health outcomes in population‐based studies after controlling for known confounders.
74
,
75
We are also aware of the potential for residual confounding by unmeasured confounders and the differential accuracy of food intake reporting by obesity status.
76
In addition, self‐reported variables like dietary intake, physical activity, and smoking status could be influenced by recall or social desirability bias. Furthermore, without considering temporal dietary or metabolic variations, we cannot rule out potential bidirectional associations between diet and metabolites. We were unable to assess how temporality may affect the reliability of the observed diet–metabolite associations. Taken together, these factors may have obscured our ability to detect significant diet–metabolite associations by obesity status. Despite these limitations, BMI performs well as an indicator of body mass for most individuals and is the standard screening tool for clinicians and researchers.
Although untargeted metabolomics comprehensively captures the widest range of metabolites associated with diet, sources of variability, including interindividual variability of foods consumed and metabolites preserved in blood plasma, may reduce power to detect metabolite–diet associations.
77
We anticipate that our missing data are a combination of missing at random and informatively missing. This uncertainty in missingness is a common issue for untargeted metabolomics. We used random forest imputation, which performs relatively well in these scenarios.
32
However, given its assumption of data missing at random, it is possible that we may have incorrectly imputed some estimates. Despite this, random forest outperforms other methods of imputation when there are different types of missingness, which is appropriate given uncertainty in identifying the exact reason or combination of reasons of missing data for each peak.
32
The metabolomics platform we used may have introduced bias by favoring robust, ubiquitous metabolites, as is common with metabolomics platforms. It is possible that certain metabolomic pathways were better preserved in fasted plasma samples than others (eg, caffeine)
60
and metabolites from episodically consumed foods (eg, stachydrine from citrus foods) may have been missed altogether.
78
,
79
Taken together, this may have overrepresented common metabolic pathways while missing transient pathways that could reveal more granular metabolic differences between groups. However, our platform also includes several unnamed compounds that may be confirmed with further interrogation.
In addition, although retention rates remained high since baseline,
27
we cannot rule out potential for selection bias, as those who were lost to follow‐up may differ from those who completed the year 20 examination. Although diet history and metabolomics data were collected nearly 20 years ago, any concerns regarding the validity of these data are outweighed by the lifecycle period of the participants (before the onset or progression of cardiovascular disease) and time period when the food environment included fewer chemical additives and processed foods. Finally, our study lacked external validation, as we were unable to use data from another cohort to replicate our findings.
Strengths
CARDIA is a large, prospective cohort with extensive diet history data, providing a strong estimation of usual diet and untargeted metabolomics data measured concurrently with diet data. Metabolomics data were collected from plasma samples within the same time period as the diet history questionnaire, which provides optimal opportunity to detect concurrent diet–metabolite relationships. Additionally, CARDIA used untargeted metabolomics, rather than targeted, which allows for hypothesis generation, elucidates potential disease mechanisms, and provides essential information about the potential for BMI modification of the association between diet quality and circulating metabolites among middle‐aged self‐reported Black and White men and women to provide critical information about biological pathways before the onset and progression of clinical cardiovascular disease in large numbers of participants.
CONCLUSIONS
Although this study did not assess causal relationships, our findings are consistent with our hypothesis that the ability of plasma metabolites to correlate with habitual diet quality differs by obesity status among middle‐aged adults, as shown in multivariable‐adjusted linear regression and OPLS‐R models. Underlying biological mechanisms for observed differences in diet–metabolite associations by obesity have not been fully elucidated. However, our study identified metabolic pathways that distinguished individuals by obesity status, namely pathways involved in polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism (eg, linoleic acid), branched‐chain amino acids (eg, leucine, isoleucine, and valine biosynthesis), and cholesterol metabolism (eg, primary bile acid biosynthesis, steroid biosynthesis, and steroid hormone biosynthesis). Our findings can help inform future research related to (1) tailoring of nutritional recommendations by obesity status, (2) potential therapeutic avenues to target specific metabolic pathways perturbed by obesity, (3) adaptation of clinical guidelines based on metabolomic data to reduce chronic disease, and (4) identification of subclassifications of obesity according to metabolic characteristics.
